statement: How much less harmful vaping is than smoking is contested, and no source read measures it: none reports how often any disease or death occurs in people who only vape, so every estimate rests on levels of chemicals in the body, short-term measurements and expert judgement. Lower exposure is not disputed in the sources read: compared with people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body (UK review, pooled analyses: breakdown products of tobacco-specific nitrosamines 58% to 94% lower), and in the National Academies' account of 15 human studies, lasting from single sessions to about two years, people who switched completely from smoking showed better short-term respiratory, cardiovascular and oral measures in all but one. What is disputed is what that shows about overall harm. On one side, the UK government-commissioned review judges its own 2015 estimate, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), still broadly accurate over the short and medium term and prefers to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking (McNeill et al., 2022); the National Academies rated the evidence of lower exposure to toxicants conclusive and of reduced short-term adverse outcomes in several organ systems substantial (the committee's judgments; National Academies, 2018). On the other, an editorial argues that the figure began as a 2013 rating by 12 experts whose own authors listed the lack of hard evidence as a limitation (as the editorial quotes it; the 2013 paper was not read), and that it should not be relied on now that devices and liquids have changed (Eissenberg et al., 2020); the Australian government-commissioned review holds that comparisons with smoking cannot establish the direct health effect of vaping, takes people who have never smoked and people who use no nicotine as the main reference, found no evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease or invasive cancer, and rated certainty low or very low for most outcomes (Banks et al., 2023). Each side concedes part of the other's case: the editorial that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the Australian review that people who switch completely and promptly may benefit; the UK review that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked, and that exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher than with using no nicotine product. The longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months, and many of its pooled biomarker results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days; the funders and interests of each source are given in the anchors and the flag note. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: People who smoke and switch completely to vaping have much lower levels of many smoke chemicals in their bodies than people who keep smoking, and in short studies their lung and heart checks did better. But how much less harmful vaping is over a whole life is argued over, and nobody has measured it yet: no study has followed people who only vape for decades to count illness or death. A UK review says the old estimate that smoking is at least 20 times more harmful still fits the short and medium term. An editorial says the estimate began as ratings by 12 experts in 2013 and should not be relied on, and an Australian review says that comparing with smoking cannot show what vaping does to health by itself. None of the sources read says vaping is risk-free, most of all for people who have never smoked, and compared with using no nicotine at all, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher.
population: Adults who smoke or have smoked and who vape or switch completely to vaping (mostly short studies); people who have never smoked and who vape; as covered by two government-commissioned reviews, a National Academies report and an editorial
exposure: Vaping nicotine e-cigarettes (alone, or replacing smoking completely)
comparator: Continuing to smoke cigarettes; and, as a second comparison, using no nicotine product
outcome: Overall harm to health, disease and death (not measured in any source read); what was measured instead: levels of chemicals in the body, short-term lung, heart and blood-pressure measures, laboratory emissions, and expert ratings
magnitude: Not estimable from the sources read: none gives the rate of any disease or death in people who only vape, against people who smoke or people who use no nicotine. The figure in dispute: vaping at least 95% less harmful than smoking, that is smoking at least 20 times more harmful, stated in the UK 2015 report and described in 2022 as broadly accurate over the short and medium term (McNeill et al., 2022); described as arising from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria (Eissenberg et al., 2020; the rating itself not read). Measured, people who vape against people who smoke (UK review, pooled analyses): nitrosamine breakdown products NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower; blood carboxyhaemoglobin lower; nicotine not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; metals mixed. Against people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher; volatile organic compounds not significantly different except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses (past smoking not separable); metals mostly higher. As described by the National Academies: smoke constituents 9- to 450-fold higher than aerosol (15 puffs assumed equal to one cigarette; Goniewicz et al., 2014); toxicants 82% to more than 99% lower per puff (Margham et al., 2016); about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents in smoke (Tayyarah and Long, 2014); 4 of 11 metals higher in one aerosol than in smoke (Williams et al., 2013); in people who switched, urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower after 5 days (105 people), NNAL down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks (20 people); all but one of the human studies showed short-term improvement, none showed more harm among people who switched. Follow-up: the UK review could summarise at most 12 months; the Australian review found no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease (21 studies) or invasive cancer (1 study).

evidence.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The UK review's authors recall that their 2015 report estimated vaping to be at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful to the person), a statement offered to help the public and professionals grasp the size of the gap. They write that summarising relative risks across many products, behaviours and biomarkers can be simplistic and misread; that, on the evidence reviewed, they judge the at-least-95% estimate still broadly accurate for the short and medium term; that it may now be more fitting to summarise their findings with their other firm statement, that vaping carries only a small share of smoking's risks; and that this does not mean vaping is free of risk, particularly for people who have never smoked. They add that the size of this gap is not reflected in current public perceptions. The pages read give no source or calculation for the 2015 figure. This is the authors' judgment on an estimate from their own earlier report.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
evidence.quote: vaping poses only a small fraction of the risks of smoking

evidence.locator: Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm
evidence.extracted: The review's overall conclusions, on the evidence it reviewed: in the short and medium term vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks; it is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects, so studies of vaping for more than 12 months are needed; more standardised methods in future studies would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than with not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: the team could draw only limited conclusions, but better-run studies of short and medium term risks found no major causes of concern associated with vaping.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Nicotine; Volatile organic compounds; Tobacco specific nitrosamines; Other potential toxicants; Carbon monoxide; Metals
evidence.extracted: The systematic review's biomarker chapter (60 studies of nicotine, 24 of volatile organic compounds, 28 of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, 9 of other toxicants, 33 of carbon monoxide and 10 of metals; designs, definitions and exposure periods varied and few studies were from the UK). People who vape compared with people who smoke, pooled analyses: nicotine and its breakdown products not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; volatile organic compound breakdown products mostly significantly lower in 15 analyses (acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower), with formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; nitrosamine breakdown products significantly lower in all 5 analyses (NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower in both analyses; metals mixed. People who vape compared with people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher, as expected (4 analyses); volatile organic compounds not significantly different in the pooled analyses except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses, which cannot separate vaping from earlier tobacco use, while a randomised trial and a cross-over study suggest levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine; metals mostly higher; carbon monoxide similar to non-use in interventional studies of people who switched completely.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Evidence reviewed, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Implications › Vaping reduces toxicant exposure compared with cigarette smoking; Methodological improvements needed; Improvements in definitions needed, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review states that studies used a range of definitions, with some classing people who vape and smoke, vape occasionally or vape daily as one group; that studies with more than one time point mostly explored acute exposure (single use to 7 days) or followed people for 8 days to 12 months, so findings on vaping for more than 12 months could not be summarised; and that few studies could be pooled. Its implications: compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure associated with cigarette smoking, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because comparisons are lacking between people who smoked for many years and have quit and now vape and those who have quit and do not vape, and with people who have never smoked or vaped; past tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers and most people who vape smoked for many years before; and no difference between people who vape and people who use no nicotine could reflect insensitive measures, background exposure, or truly similar exposure.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Implications › More research needed on biomarkers of exposure among vapers, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review states that in its meta-analyses many findings were from tobacco industry-funded randomised trials conducted in confinement (closed settings such as research centres or hospitals) for periods of up to 7 days, and that future research needs to include more independent research on biomarkers of exposure in people who vape, people who smoke and people who use no tobacco or nicotine, outside confinement and with longer follow-up. The pages read do not say how many pooled results these trials make up or whether their results differ from the independent studies.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8: Biomarkers of potential harm › Main findings › Inflammation; Endothelial function, last paragraph; Implications › Need to distinguish biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review covered 41 studies (43 publications) of oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function and platelet activation; most assessed acute vaping effects and most had methodological concerns. Inflammation: pooled cross-sectional studies showed lower blood C-reactive protein and sICAM-1 in people who vape than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this. Endothelial function: acute sessions of vaping (with and without nicotine) and of smoking produced similar short-term reductions in flow-mediated dilation, while a single randomised trial found that switching from smoking to vaping for 4 weeks significantly improved it; the review writes that acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking, and that switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. It concludes that most studies in the chapter cannot inform medium or long term risks through these biomarkers, and that studies are needed with people who use no nicotine as a comparison group and longer follow-up.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 9: Cancers › Main findings › Toxicants and carcinogens; Cancer risks; Inflammation and oxidative stress; Cell and animal studies; Implications › Longer follow up periods are needed
evidence.extracted: The review's cancer chapter calls the exposure-biomarker studies conclusive evidence that vaping generally leads to lower exposure to many of the carcinogens responsible for the health risks of smoking (exposure, not cancer). It adds that the National Academies found no available evidence on whether the chemicals in vaping aerosols or vaping behaviour were associated with cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use; that evidence on inflammation and oxidative stress is insufficient for conclusions; that no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; and that cell and animal studies suggest vaping aerosols are not benign for people who have never smoked while also suggesting alterations in gene expression to a lower extent than tobacco smoke, though translating such studies to human risk is challenging. Its implications: studies of exposure biomarkers need longer follow-up to tell whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking.

evidence.locator: Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Heart rate; Blood pressure; Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness; Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Implications, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular disease between people who use no nicotine, tobacco, or vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 16 › introductory paragraphs, 2nd paragraph; Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 1 › Issues addressed, 3rd paragraph and its list; Authors and citation
evidence.extracted: The review's closing chapter states that, despite the increase in research on vaping since 2015, weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups studied and exposure, and study designs all limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Its 61 evidence statements broadly follow the National Academies' definitions of level of evidence, and the authors write that, as the National Academies noted, the framework is a guide and a great deal of expert judgement, here by the report's co-authors, is involved. The scope left out two questions: vaping and later smoking (a Cochrane review of people under 30 was examining it) and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking (covered in the series' previous report and by a Cochrane living review). The report is the eighth in a series described as independent and commissioned by Public Health England and then the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; it was led by academics at King's College London with international collaborators (eight authors are named); the pages read carry no competing-interest statement.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, four studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes (three laboratory studies and one comparison based on published literature). Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched from Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes to E-Cigarettes › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 11th paragraphs (Cravo; 5-day study; Goniewicz; McRobbie; Shahab); Synthesis; Conclusion 18-1
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 8 months; examples: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched… › Health Risk Profile (Carnevale; Cibella; Flouris; Wadia), Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure (Martin), Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis (after the animal studies); Conclusion 18-2
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one flow measure (forced expiratory flow 25-75%) that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); and gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016). A cross-sectional study, a design the Methods say was left out of the 15, compared nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither: immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes and none found them more harmful than cigarettes. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › opening section, 4th paragraph; Evidence Review: Levels of Evidence Available, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described in the chapter's opening, the committee writes that e-cigarettes have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe, and that the evidence reviewed in the report suggests they may be less harmful than combustible cigarettes in at least some scenarios. It adds that, because the efficacy of e-cigarettes to actually reduce harm remains unclear, some researchers have raised concerns, citing McKee and Capewell (2015): continued use of a substance with its own potential health risks (including uncertainty about long-term risks), a possible increase in use of conventional tobacco products through starting and relapse, and questionable terms of engagement with the tobacco industry. The chapter states that epidemiological studies and randomised trials of the long-term health effects of exclusive e-cigarette use would give the strongest evidence of harm reduction and that, in their absence, the committee looks at biomarkers of disease and exposure levels. The chapter gives no overall figure for how much less harmful e-cigarettes are. The McKee and Capewell editorial itself was not read.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently with Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes (Dual Users) › Synthesis; Conclusions 18-3 and 18-4
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, for people who keep smoking while also using e-cigarettes (dual use) the committee found limited evidence on patterns of use and a lack of evidence on exposure and health outcomes among those who do not reduce their smoking. People with dual use did not on average smoke fewer cigarettes than people who smoked only, although e-cigarettes may help some of them maintain a reduction in smoking; the committee writes that it is very unlikely that people who do not reduce smoking after starting e-cigarettes will reduce the health risks of smoking, and that they may be exposed to additional adverse effects of e-cigarettes. Conclusion 18-3: no available evidence whether or not long-term dual use changes illness or death compared with smoking only. Conclusion 18-4: insufficient evidence that e-cigarette use changes short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems in people who continue to smoke. These are the committee's judgments.

evidence.locator: Opening section (before the first heading), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; References 1 to 3
evidence.extracted: The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.

evidence.locator: Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping to more nicotine and other toxicants and people nearby to more of any harmful aerosol constituents, and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and, relative to free-base nicotine, are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is cited in the text for the statements on power, flavours or dependence; reference 4 (Jackler and Ramamurthi, 2019, not read) is cited for the marketing of protonated nicotine liquids and the 'nicotine arms race'; the online Appendix A, a nonexhaustive list of evidence of harm, was not read.

evidence.locator: Second headed section (harm to cells), 1st paragraph; third headed section (harm in people), 1st paragraph; references 5 and 6
evidence.extracted: The authors state that e-cigarette aerosols contain toxicants and are harmful to living cells in vitro and in vivo (volatile aldehydes, carcinogenic furans, chloropropanols and acetal compounds are named) and that animals exposed to aerosol show adverse effects, including in cardiovascular models (no source cited). For people they cite one report of airway epithelial injury in healthy young adults who smoked cigarettes occasionally and used an e-cigarette with or without nicotine (two randomised trials, Chaumont et al., 2019); state without a citation that wheezing has been associated with use and that heart rate, blood pressure and platelet activation rise while flow-mediated dilation and heart rate variability fall; and cite a one-page item in a journal supplement (reference 6, a conference abstract by its citation), which they call a preliminary report, for a possibly higher risk of heart attack and coronary artery disease in people who vape. The section headings state harm categorically; the conclusion speaks of potential harm.

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Increase Smoking Risk, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors quote the National Academies' conclusion of substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people and young adults, and argue that, to the extent that first use of e-cigarettes causes later smoking in someone who would otherwise never have smoked, vaping could be considered as harmful as smoking for that person. The statement is conditional on causation and concerns a person who would not otherwise have smoked, not the comparison of vaping with smoking in people who already smoke.

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants sometimes differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.

evidence.locator: Conclusions; Call to Action
evidence.extracted: Conclusion: the 2013 estimate, which lacked evidence, cannot be valid today and should not be relied upon further; future estimates should rest on the evidence now available and be revised as evidence accrues. The call to action calls the 95% safer estimate a factoid, unreliable information repeated until accepted as fact, and asks readers to highlight its unreliable provenance, the changes in devices and liquids, the accumulation of evidence of potential harm, the increased prevalence of use and the growing evidence that e-cigarette use is associated with later smoking. The editorial gives no alternative figure and does not weigh the evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch: it is an argument, with no data, search or appraisal of the studies it cites.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflicts of Interests
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration; the sponsor had no role in the preparation of the work. Interests as printed: two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and are named on a patent for a device that measures the puffing behaviour of people who use electronic cigarettes; one of them has also, since September 2019, been a consultant in litigation against the electronic cigarette industry; another author reports personal fees from Hydra Biosciences LLC and Sanofi SA and non-financial support from GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work. No tobacco or vape industry funding of the editorial is stated.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Data sources, Data synthesis; Methods › 1st paragraph; Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all, registered in advance; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted.

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, rows 'Cardiovascular disease (21)', 'Cancer (1)' and 'Respiratory disease (58)'; the three paragraphs after Box 3
evidence.extracted: Australian review, Box 3 (health outcome, number of studies): cardiovascular disease (21 studies): clinical outcomes such as heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death, and subclinical atherosclerosis: no available evidence; other cardiovascular outcomes in people who smoke: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely increase heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term nicotine e-cigarette use after switching from smoking reduces blood pressure; in people who do not smoke, insufficient evidence. Cancer (1 study): invasive cancer and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence. Respiratory disease (58 studies): asthma, bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: insufficient evidence in people who smoke and none for people who do not; reduced exacerbations or progression in people who smoke and switch: insufficient evidence. The review states that evidence is insufficient or unavailable on cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory conditions other than lung injury and most other conditions, and rated the certainty of evidence for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully overcome, particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful when discussing the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; it writes that risks of bias were noted across health outcomes, but significant concerns in other domains meant they were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation or the overall certainty of evidence. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that a key finding of its synthesis was the general paucity of evidence on the effects of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarettes on many major clinical outcomes, including cancer, cardiovascular, metabolic, mental health, developmental, reproductive and neurological outcomes (other than seizures). It describes an English review it found after its search (reference 40, the UK review of 2022) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, as focusing on comparing the effects of e-cigarette use with those of smoking and on biomarkers, and as generally finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. It concludes that its findings concur broadly with those of other major reviews, including that the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review notes that in many countries dual smoking and e-cigarette use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use and that the direct health impact of dual use is unknown. It writes that e-cigarettes may be beneficial for people who smoke who use them to quit completely and promptly, but that the limited evidence, their risks, uncertainty about effects on major clinical outcomes and continued smoking by most people who use them leave their overall safety and efficacy unclear. Its conclusions: strong or conclusive evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes can be harmful to health, particularly for people who do not smoke and for children and adolescents (a statement not framed against smoking); evidence for effects on most important health outcomes uncertain; people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit.

evidence.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Box 4, row 'Smoking uptake (28)'; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review names this, with poisoning, dependence (addiction) and toxicity from inhalation, among the risks that disproportionately affect people who do not smoke and young people. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Competing interests; Methods, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding and interests as printed: the review was conducted as part of an independent programme examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes, funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC); the report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Australian Department of Health and went through an independent methodological review as part of standard NHMRC processes; competing interests: no relevant disclosures. The work also provided evidence for the 2021 update of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners smoking cessation guidelines and a 2022 statement of the NHMRC Chief Executive Officer.

risk_of_bias.note: The 95% figure began as an expert rating (known here only through the editorial's account); the UK review's pooled biomarker results include many tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days and most of its studies had methodological concerns; the National Academies' human studies were mostly small and several tested a manufacturer's own product (the chapter does not say who funded them); the editorial appraises nothing (card sc_eissenberg_2020: overall high) and the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and excluded biomarker studies. The reviews are read as summaries, not at the study level.

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the sides read a largely shared body of evidence differently and answer different questions (exposure and short-term measures against clinical outcomes and starting to smoke); the exposure findings themselves point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is lifetime harm (disease and death). What is measured is exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements (single sessions to 12 months in the UK review; to about two years in the National Academies' studies) and expert ratings; products have changed since most of the studies and newer ones are little studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate of harm is pooled, so precision is not rated.

grade.reasoning: Observational, indirect evidence (exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements and expert judgement) starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the size of the difference, which is what the sources support, with the direction (lower exposure to smoke toxicants) reported beside it. The National Academies' conclusive and substantial ratings concern exposure and short-term outcomes in people who switched completely, not lifetime harm; the UK review's statement is an expert judgment on a body of evidence that reaches only 12 months, as its authors say, and the Australian review's reading rests on a different set of evidence. Overlapping reports are counted once.

debate.question: How much less harmful than smoking is vaping: does the evidence support the often-quoted figure of at least 95% less harmful (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), and can anyone show the size of the difference yet?
debate.evidence_yes: The UK government-commissioned review (McNeill et al., 2022, King's College London, commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities) states that, on the evidence it reviewed, its own 2015 estimate that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking remains broadly accurate over the short and medium term, and that it may now be better to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking. Under that sits its systematic review of exposure biomarkers: against people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels in pooled analyses of nitrosamine breakdown products (58% to 94% lower), of acrolein, acrylonitrile and butadiene breakdown products (71%, 94% and 83% lower) and of blood carboxyhaemoglobin, with nicotine levels not different in people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; the better-run studies of short and medium term effects found no major causes of concern; immediately after use vaping raised heart rate less than smoking; in longer cross-sectional studies blood pressure was lower in people who vaped than in people who smoked; and the review expects cardiovascular risk to be much less than that of smoking from the toxicant profile (an expectation, not a measurement). The National Academies (2018, chapter 18, as the committee describes it) rated as conclusive the evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens, and as substantial the evidence that completely switching reduces short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems: all but one of the human studies it reviewed, lasting from single sessions to about two years, showed short-term improvement and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched; laboratory emissions of smoke constituents were 9- to 450-fold higher than of aerosol, toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff, and 21 of 27 cell studies and 3 of 5 animal studies favoured e-cigarettes. Even the critics grant part of this: the editorial says there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and the Australian review says people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit.
debate.evidence_no: A six-author editorial in the American Journal of Public Health (Eissenberg et al., 2020; funding and interests as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products; two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and named on a patent for a puffing-behaviour device, one of them also a consultant in litigation against the e-cigarette industry since September 2019; one author reports fees from two pharmaceutical companies) argues that the figure came from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria whose own authors listed the lack of hard evidence for most harms of most products on most criteria as a limitation (as the editorial quotes; the 2013 paper was not read), that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians nonetheless endorsed it, that devices and liquids have changed (power output 10 to 20 times higher in many devices, thousands of flavours, nicotine salts), that evidence of potential harm from cell, animal and short-term human studies has accumulated, that lower toxicant content in aerosol does not by itself show lower lethality, and that the estimate cannot be valid today; it offers no alternative figure and cites a conference abstract for its heart-attack claim. The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures) holds that comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes, that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify effects and people who neither smoke nor vape the main comparison group, that evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease and invasive cancer is not available, and that certainty is very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes; it rates acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure after nicotine e-cigarette use in people who smoke as moderate evidence. The National Academies state that e-cigarettes have not been proven safe, give no overall figure for how much less harmful they are, say that long-term epidemiological studies and randomised trials would be the strongest evidence and are lacking, and describe concerns raised by McKee and Capewell (2015) about continued use of a product with its own risks, more use of conventional tobacco products and engagement with the tobacco industry (that editorial itself was not read). The UK review itself says that, against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher; that the degree of any residual risk remains unclear; that acute vaping might impair blood-vessel function as much as acute smoking; that its findings reach at most 12 months of follow-up; and that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked.
debate.neither_can_show: No source read reports how often any disease, or death, occurs in people who only vape compared with people who smoke or who use no nicotine: the UK review could summarise follow-up of no more than 12 months and says the size of any residual risk is unclear; it and the Australian review each report no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes such as heart attack and stroke, and no evidence on cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use (UK, quoting the National Academies) or on invasive cancer (Australian). The 95% figure was an expert rating across several criteria, not a ratio of disease rates (as the editorial describes it; the 2013 paper and the 2015 report were not read, and the UK pages read give no basis for the 2015 figure), and the UK review's reaffirmation is its own judgment from biomarker evidence, not a measured ratio. A level of a chemical in the body is not a risk: a 90% lower level of a carcinogen breakdown product does not by itself give a 90% lower risk of cancer. Most people who vape smoked for many years before, and past smoking changes many biomarkers; no study read compares people who smoked for many years and quit, whether or not they now vape, or follows people who vape and have never smoked for years, so neither the comparison with smoking nor the comparison with using no nicotine can be made cleanly. The two reviews do not weigh the same evidence: the UK review rests mainly on exposure and potential-harm biomarkers, which the Australian review excluded, while the Australian review asks about clinical outcomes (and about starting to smoke, which the UK review left to a Cochrane review) and takes people who use no nicotine as its main comparison. Both are government-commissioned and both rest on judgment: the UK authors assess an estimate stated in their own earlier series of reports (three of the eight 2022 authors are among the six named for the 2015 report in the editorial's reference list) and say a great deal of expert judgement is involved in their evidence statements; many of their pooled results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days, with independent work still called for; the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and assumed products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were nicotine e-cigarettes; the editorial argues one side with no data, and its authors' interests are as printed above. In many countries the most frequent pattern is to vape while still smoking (the Australian review), and the National Academies found no evidence on the long-term health of people who do so; products have changed since most of these studies and newer ones are little studied.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read so far (the Australian review and the editorial read in full; a National Academies chapter and the UK review's summary pages as they describe the studies), two things are reported consistently: against people who smoke, people who vape have much lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body and, in people who switched completely, better short-term measures of breathing and circulation, although some short-term effects, such as blood-vessel function after a single session, were similar to smoking; and nobody has measured how much the rates of disease and death differ. Against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher. Neither the lower exposure nor the lack of long-term data is disputed in the sources read; the editorial disputes only that lower toxicant content by itself shows lower lethality. What is disputed is whether the old at least 20-fold figure, which began as an expert rating, can still stand as a size: the UK review says it broadly does for the short and medium term, as its own judgment; the editorial and the Australian review say it cannot be relied on. The strongest argument for the figure is the consistency and size of the exposure reductions across independent pooled analyses and the finding that no study showed more harm in people who switched completely; the strongest against is that none of this is a rate of disease, the longest follow-up summarised was a year, and the pooled evidence rests on measurements of chemicals in the body, some from industry-funded trials. The editors offer no number: any figure would claim more than the sources show, and both halves belong together: much lower exposure to smoke toxicants than smoking, and not risk-free.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that follow people for decades with biologically verified use and count disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who smoked and have quit with and without vaping, people who both smoke and vape, and people who have never used nicotine, reported as absolute risks so that the difference can be read directly; independent biomarker studies outside confinement, with follow-up beyond 12 months and agreed biomarkers and definitions (the UK review's own list); a transparent, repeatable estimate that sets out the outcomes, their weights and the evidence for each, updated for current devices and liquids and pre-registered (as the editorial calls for); and trials or natural experiments comparing people who switch completely with people who keep smoking on clinical outcomes. None of the sources read reports any of these: the longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months and the longest in the National Academies chapter was about two years.
